clue.text: Dicky in business …

parts.note: taken as written
a firm is a business

explanation.surface: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue, as if someone shaky were in business with a man called Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky is informal British for weak or unsound, as in a dicky heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone frail and in poor health, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Domestic crime in incidental book

parts.note: taken as written
a side issue is an incidental one
Job is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A household crime mentioned in passing in some novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Domestic' means within the household or firm, not family violence.
explanation.definitionFit: An inside job is a crime committed by someone within the organisation or household itself.

clue.text: Removes the impurities from contaminated trifles

indicators.note: contaminated things are spoilt and mixed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: A cook cleans up some spoiled trifle desserts.
explanation.walkthrough: A trifle is a British layered pudding of sponge, custard and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Filtering a liquid strains out unwanted particles, purifying it.

clue.text: Russian naval officer, a flier

parts.note: Red was a common label for a Soviet Russian
an admiral commands a fleet

explanation.surface: A Soviet fleet commander who is also an aviator.
explanation.walkthrough: The flier is not a pilot but an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The red admiral is a common European butterfly with red bands on dark wings, so it flies.

clue.text: … with Bill, strange to tell

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
quaint means oddly old-fashioned, strange

explanation.surface: Read with the previous clue: a sickly man in business with Bill, an odd story to relate.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquaint someone with a fact is to inform them of it, so it means to tell.

clue.text: Raffles a joker?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Raffles, the gentleman safe-breaker of E. W. Hornung's stories
second meaning, whimsical: a crack is a quip, so a man of cracks

explanation.walkthrough: Raffles is a fictional Victorian gentleman burglar; the question mark flags the punning second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A cracksman is a burglar who breaks open safes, which is what Raffles did.

clue.text: Found out it's partly open

indicators.note: partly means only a portion of the words is taken

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone has been exposed, though only half of it is out in the open.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a lock, button or parcel is to unfasten or open it.

clue.text: When bird visits islands up in the Arctic, it can be dangerous

definitions.text: in the Arctic, it can be dangerous

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters climb, read from bottom to top

parts.note: a grebe is a diving water bird
CI stands for the Channel Islands; visits means joins

explanation.surface: A water bird drops in on some islands in the Arctic, where danger lurks.
explanation.definitionFit: Floating masses of frozen sea ice are a notorious hazard to polar shipping.

clue.text: From the very first time, everyone says that you're cantankerous

indicators.note: the very first of each word means only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: Everyone has said you were grumpy from the very beginning.
explanation.definitionFit: Testy and cantankerous both mean irritable and quick to take offence.

clue.text: Prominent person turns up here — to get a divorce?

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word is read from the bottom upward

parts.note: a oner is British slang for an outstanding person

explanation.surface: A celebrity arrives somewhere, perhaps to end a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: A oner is an old British term for someone remarkable.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nevada city was famous for quick, easy divorces after a short residency.

clue.text: Little money invested in second dwelling, an untidy spot …

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece goes within the others

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
P, a penny, is a small coin
a lodge is a small house

explanation.surface: Someone sinks a little cash into a second home, and the result is a messy blot.
explanation.walkthrough: The penny goes inside the S-plus-LODGE pair, just after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A splodge is a blot or smear, a messy mark of ink or paint.

clue.text: … a dwelling in readiness

definitions.meaning: second meaning: skill or dexterity, an older sense of the word

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the old one of adroitness, as in 'handled it with address'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a house's location and also, in an older usage, deftness or prompt skill.

clue.text: Shrink from adopting footballer's hairstyle

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so one word holds another inside it

parts.note: to dread something is to shrink from it
a lock is a forward in rugby football

explanation.surface: A man recoils from a footballer's hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: The footballer plays rugby: a lock is a second-row forward, and the 's is part of the hairstyle's possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreadlocks are long matted ropes of hair, a style worn especially by Rastafarians.

clue.text: Group in need of a drink, by the sound of it

indicators.note: the phrase asks us to listen to the word rather than read its spelling

parts.note: bevvy is British slang for an alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: A group of people who badly need a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A bevvy is British slang for a drink, usually beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bevy is a gathering or company, traditionally of girls or of quail.

clue.text: After operation, one is unable to stop laughing

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sewn up after surgery

explanation.surface: A patient after surgery who cannot stop giggling.
explanation.walkthrough: The surgical sense is literal; the laughter sense is an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone convulsed with mirth, and literally a surgical wound is closed with sutures.

clue.text: James has to dig a hole for shrub

parts.note: Jas is the old written abbreviation for James
to mine is to excavate

explanation.surface: A gardener called James must dig a hole to plant a shrub.
explanation.definitionFit: Jasmine is a climbing shrub with fragrant white or yellow flowers.

clue.text: Seven eels stewed to provide refreshments

indicators.note: stewing breaks food down and mixes it, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: A cook stews seven eels as a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is the British mid-morning snack or tea break.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is light food and drink taken around eleven in the morning, a break for refreshment.

clue.text: Old chap in front was a runner

indicators.note: being in front means one word is placed before the other

parts.note: a chap is a man
aged means old

explanation.surface: An elderly man led a race as the front runner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' is the man who runs a business, not an athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: To run a company is to direct it, so someone who ran things directed and controlled them.

clue.text: Happy being darkened? Not really

definitions.meaning: second meaning, playful: with the lights taken away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not really' admits the second sense is a pun: DE- as a removal prefix before LIGHTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Delighted means greatly pleased, a stronger synonym of glad.

clue.text: Dressing, forsooth, with collar back to front

indicators.note: back to front means the joined words are read from their last letter to their first

parts.note: egad and forsooth are both archaic exclamations
to collar a suspect is to nab or arrest them

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in dismay because a shirt collar has been put on back to front while dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole joined string is reversed, not just the collar.
explanation.definitionFit: In first aid a dressing is the wrapping strip applied to protect an injury, the same thing named another way.

clue.text: Moonies can become offensive

indicators.note: can become signals the letters turning into something else

parts.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: Members of the Unification Church may turn unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Moonies are followers of Sun Myung Moon's Unification Church.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means foul-smelling or disgusting, so it is offensive to the senses.

clue.text: The game's rigged, bent completely

indicators.note: something rigged is tampered with, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before the rearranging
all means completely, as in all wrong

explanation.surface: A complaint that the match is fixed and utterly corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' reads as crooked, which suits the surface, but it is the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Netball is a team sport, played mainly by women in Britain, in which goals are scored through a high ring.

clue.text: A doctor attending eastern president upset by tiny organisms

parts.note: taken as written
MO is a medical officer

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads upward

parts.note: Abe Lincoln, the US president
E is the abbreviation for eastern

explanation.surface: A doctor treating an Eastern head of state who is laid low by microbes.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the president is turned over, and he sits before the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Amoebae are single-celled microscopic creatures, so they are tiny living organisms.

clue.text: Piano accompaniment to song, a duet

parts.note: p is the musical marking for piano, softly
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A piano part accompanying a song sung by two voices.
explanation.definitionFit: A duet is performed by two people, and two together make a couple or twosome.

clue.text: Birdseed —- just what you wanted!

parts.note: a pip is a fruit seed
it means the very thing, as in 'that's it'

explanation.surface: A delighted gift of birdseed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birdseed' looks like one word but splits: Bird is the definition and seed starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipit is a small brown songbird, such as the meadow pipit.

clue.text: The dragon's resolved to be stubborn

indicators.note: resolved can mean broken down and re-formed, so the letters are rebuilt

parts.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale dragon has made up its mind to be obstinate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolved' reads as determined, which matches the definition's mood, but here it signals the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A headstrong person insists on their own way and refuses advice, which is obstinacy.

clue.text: Weakling has swim across river

indicators.note: lying across something means stretching over it, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a dip is a quick swim
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A feeble person attempts to swim across a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A drip is informal for a dull, feeble, spineless person.

clue.text: Mole is said to see with difficulty

indicators.note: is said points to a spoken word, judged by ear

parts.note: a mole is a stone breakwater or jetty

explanation.surface: A mole, being nearly blind, is said to struggle to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' is not the burrowing animal but a harbour wall.
explanation.definitionFit: To peer is to look closely, squinting, as when vision is poor.

clue.text: Claim of journalists concealed

indicators.note: something concealed is kept inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: the press are journalists collectively
taken as written

explanation.surface: A claim made by reporters that has been hushed up.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'of' is the one hidden inside the journalists.
explanation.definitionFit: To profess something is to declare or assert it openly, often falsely.

clue.text: Live like a nun

wordplay.note: a nun dresses in a habit

explanation.surface: Living the life of a nun.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay splits as IN HABIT, the robe a nun wears.
explanation.definitionFit: To inhabit a place is to dwell or reside there.

clue.text: Man put in to improve project

indicators.note: putting something in means placing it inside another word

parts.note: to rise is to get better
he is a male pronoun

explanation.surface: A man is brought on board to rescue a struggling project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' looks like a noun but is the verb, to put forward an idea.
explanation.definitionFit: To project an idea is to propose or speculate, which is forming a theory.

clue.text: Ringway to terminate in port

parts.note: the letter O is ring-shaped
ST is short for street, a way
to end is to terminate

explanation.surface: Travellers heading out of Ringway, once the name of Manchester Airport, for a sea port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringway' is one word in the clue, the old name of Manchester Airport, but splits into Ring and way.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostend is a Belgian ferry port on the North Sea coast.
